g.text: No isolation level below SERIALIZABLE prevents this - so 'we use transactions' is not an answer
The danger lives in the GAP between the SELECT and the UPDATE, where application code decided on data that went stale before it was written back.
Two races that get conflated constantly - and need completely different mechanisms
RACE A one user, two clicks
The user hits Book twice, or the browser resubmits after a
submit #2 -> INSERT INTO reservation (...) -> UNIQUE VIOLATION
-> handler catches it, returns the ORIGINAL reservation
Two details make it work. The id is generated by the CLIENT before
the first attempt - if the server minted it on receipt, each retry
would get a fresh id and look like a new booking; the id has to be
born with the FORM, not with the request. And it is a UNIQUE
CONSTRAINT, not a SELECT first: checking 'does this id exist?' before
inserting is a check-then-act race, and only the database's unique
Disabling the button client-side is worth doing and is NOT a
solution: it fails with JavaScript off, on a double-tap that fires
before the handler, and on a browser-level resubmit.
RACE B two users, one room
Two different people submit bookings for the last available room at
UPDATE ... SET total_reserved = 100 UPDATE ... SET total_reserved = 100
One booking has silently vanished from the count, so the hotel will sell
that room again. And READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ both PERMIT this,
because nothing was read inconsistently - both transactions read a
A is solved by idempotency. B is solved by concurrency control. NEITHER MECHANISM SOLVES THE OTHER, and shipping only one of
Four ways to close the gap
1 pessimistic - lock the row before reading it
FOR UPDATE; -- transaction 2 now BLOCKS here
Correct by construction, and the BEST option under heavy contention: a lock queue makes steady progress
while optimistic approaches burn CPU on rollbacks. The costs are real, though. Locks are held for the
WHOLE transaction, so the transaction must contain nothing slow - which is exactly why payment sits
outside it. Multi-night bookings lock several rows, so two bookings with overlapping, differently-
ordered date ranges can DEADLOCK - mitigated by always locking in date order, which the range scan gives
naturally, but the application must still handle a deadlock rollback and retry. And a FOR UPDATE over a
14-night stay locks 14 rows, blocking any overlapping booking even for a single night that is not
2 optimistic - take no lock, detect at write time
WHERE hotel_id=245 AND room_type_id=1001 AND date='2026-06-01';
WHERE hotel_id=245 AND ... AND version = 42; -- the GUARD
-- affected rows == 0 => someone else won => retry or 409
CHECKING THE AFFECTED ROW COUNT IS THE ENTIRE MECHANISM - forgetting to check it is how this pattern
silently fails in real codebases, because the UPDATE 'succeeds' having changed nothing. Use a version
INTEGER, not a timestamp: timestamps suffer clock skew between application servers and insufficient
resolution, so two updates in the same millisecond look unchanged.
No locks, so readers never block, and it is faster than pessimistic when conflicts are rare - which
describes the vast majority of this system's traffic, since most hotels on most dates have plenty of
rooms. But it degrades badly under high contention, because transactions repeatedly do work and throw it
away. A ROLLBACK STORM is worse than a lock queue: burning CPU to make no progress - and that is exactly
3 a database constraint - move the invariant into the schema
No SELECT, no version column, no explicit lock: a single UPDATE is atomic and takes its own brief row
lock automatically, so the stale-read window is gone because there is no separate read. The simplest
correct thing - and, importantly, THE INVARIANT IS ENFORCED AGAINST EVERY CODE PATH, including a buggy
new service, a data migration, or a manual UPDATE during an incident. It is the only option that cannot
be bypassed by forgetting to use it. Against that: constraints are not version-controlled alongside
application code the way logic is, not every database supports CHECK with expressions, and it yields a
generic constraint violation rather than a domain error, so the application must translate it.
4 the atomic conditional UPDATE - put the rule in the WHERE clause
Not in the standard three, and often the best answer. NO READ-THEN-WRITE GAP, so the lost update is
structurally impossible rather than detected. No version column to maintain and no retry loop to write
or tune. The business rule AND the atomicity are the same expression, so you cannot forget to apply the
overbooking limit - it is the thing making the write conditional. And the affected-row count carries the
multi-night semantics for free: fewer rows updated than nights requested means some night was full,
which is exactly what the 409 needs.
This applies here only because inventory is a COUNTER, not a unique resource. A seat-booking system,
where each seat is a distinct resource with a binary state, cannot use it and has to fall back to
Choosing - and keeping a mechanism that should never fire
No read-then-write gap, no retry loop, no version column, and it
encodes the overbooking rule in the same expression that provides
the atomicity. It performs well under both low and high contention,
and the affected-row count gives multi-night correctness for free.
Kept even though option 4 makes it unreachable, because it is the only
mechanism no code path can bypass. Its job changes from 'enforce the rule'
to 'MAKE A BUG IN THE ENFORCEMENT LOUD' - the same defence-in-depth
reasoning as the URL shortener's retained unique index. And because it
should never trigger, an alert on any violation is meaningful.
Plus UNIQUE(reservation_id) for Race A, which is orthogonal.
Why not pessimistic, given that contention is the real load profile and pessimistic is best under contention? Because option
4's lock is held for the duration of ONE STATEMENT - microseconds - so there is no meaningful contention window left to queue
on. Pessimistic locking wins when the TRANSACTION is long, and the whole point of moving payment outside the transaction was
to make it short. Having done that, the lock-free option is strictly better.
When pessimistic WOULD be right: if the booking decision genuinely required application logic that cannot be expressed in SQL
- a fraud check, a loyalty-tier calculation, a multi-room-type group booking with cross-type rules. Then you need the read and
the write in the same guarded window, and FOR UPDATE is the tool. Group bookings are named elsewhere as unbuilt, so this is
And why not SERIALIZABLE? It would work - it prevents the lost update outright. But it costs throughput across EVERY
transaction in the database, not just contended ones; in PostgreSQL it is implemented optimistically, so you still get
serialization failures and still need retry handling; and it is a blunt global setting for a problem localized to one row's
update. Option 4 solves it for the price of one WHERE clause.
